horizon_driver: Actuarial valuation cycle (triennial UK, annual US) plus funded-status reporting to trustees/boards dominates decision cadence, even though underlying liabilities run 12-25+ years in duration (average pension liability duration ~12.8yr per BAML Mature/Average US Pension Plan indices, cited in Wilshire's June 2026 funding status release). Insurers additionally run quarterly rating-agency and Solvency II/RBC capital reviews.

constraints.source: Bank of England FPC statement 29 Mar 2023 + TPR guidance 24 Apr 2023 requiring UK DB schemes to hold a minimum 250bps market-stress buffer in leveraged LDI, replenishable within 5 days (https://www.thepensionsregulator.gov.uk, via Travers Smith/WTW summaries 2023)
constraints.breaks_under: sponsor covenant deterioration forces trustees to chase return over safety, or funding ratio falls fast enough that the buffer itself cannot be replenished in the 5-day window (as happened Sep-Oct 2022 before the rule existed)

constraints.source: BlackRock exited the Net Zero Asset Managers initiative 9 Jan 2025 citing 'confusion regarding practices' and 'legal inquiries from public officials'; NZAM suspended all activities and removed its signatory list from 13 Jan 2025 pending review (ESGdive, AI-CIO, benefitspro, Jan 2025)
constraints.breaks_under: US political/legal pressure exceeds the reputational cost of exit; observed to break already at scale in Jan 2025 across BlackRock, State Street, and most large US managers within the Net Zero Banking Alliance/NZAM ecosystem

constraints.source: CalPERS raised its private-markets target from 33% to 40% of the total fund (Mar 2024 policy) and doubled its private-credit target from 5% to 8% (Sep 2024 asset allocation review), reaching ~$24bn/4.2% private debt by May 2026 even as the broader private-credit market entered its 'most challenging environment since 2008' (Pensions & Investments, Connect Money, withintelligence.com, 2026)
constraints.breaks_under: manager return-chasing under benchmark/peer pressure overrides stated prudence and liquidity-policy limits; already visible industry-wide — institutional LP allocations to private credit averaged 6.8% of portfolios in 2025 vs 3.1% in 2019

stated_vs_revealed.stated: Pension schemes and insurers frame long-duration bond/LDI holdings as prudent, low-risk liability matching undertaken purely for beneficiary safety, overseen by fiduciary trustees.
stated_vs_revealed.revealed: UK DB schemes ran leveraged LDI overlays (pre-2022, unregulated leverage ratios) that turned a hedging tool into a systemic amplifier: the Sep 2022 gilt sell-off forced LDI funds into fire-sales of gilts to meet margin/collateral calls, contributing roughly half of the total decline in long gilt prices and forcing a Bank of England emergency purchase programme of up to £65bn (28 Sep 2022, confirmed in IMF Working Paper 2023/210 and Bank Underground, 2024). 'Liability matching' was materially leveraged speculation on rate stability.
stated_vs_revealed.delta: Large. The stated purpose (hedging) and the revealed mechanism (leveraged, procyclical, systemically destabilising under a 100bp/4-day yield move) diverge sharply — and only broke into regulatory correction (TPR/FCA resilience buffers) after the event, not before.

stated_vs_revealed.stated: Pension funds describe themselves as patient, fiduciary-bound long-term capital seeking safety and diversification for beneficiaries, subject to strict liquidity and credit-quality policies.
stated_vs_revealed.revealed: With funded ratios strongly in surplus in 2026 (Milliman 100 PFI 112.1% at end-July 2026; Wilshire ~108.7-110% through mid-2026), sponsors are using the freed-up risk budget not to further de-risk into duration but to chase yield into private credit and other illiquid alternatives — CalPERS, CalSTRS, Arkansas Teachers, New Mexico SWF and Virginia's pension all added to private-credit stakes through the March 2026 'private credit meltdown' rather than retreating (Pensions & Investments, Connect Money, Fortune, 2026).
stated_vs_revealed.delta: The Cartographer's premise that AM_ACTIVE duration demand is a 'forced flow, mechanically certain' understates how funded-status surplus actually reduces forced buying and instead funds discretionary risk-taking in a much less transparent asset class — the forced-flow logic applies asymmetrically (mainly when underfunded), and 2026 conditions are the opposite case.

tripwires.if: aggregate funded ratio for major DB systems falls below ~90% within a single quarter (reversing the 2026 surplus)
tripwires.then: forced, price-insensitive duration buying resumes at scale and dominates behaviour over yield-chasing, reproducing the pre-2022 'mechanically certain flow' the Cartographer describes

tripwires.if: long-gilt or long-Treasury yields move >100bps within a 3-5 day window
tripwires.then: leveraged LDI/duration overlays face margin calls that can force fire-sales large enough to require central-bank intervention, as in Sep-Oct 2022, despite post-2023 resilience buffers (250bps minimum, 5-day replenishment) narrowing but not eliminating this risk

tripwires.if: a major private-credit manager (top-5 AUM) is forced to mark down a concentrated sector exposure (e.g., AI/software-heavy books flagged by BIS Mar 2026 Quarterly Review)
tripwires.then: insurer and pension LPs holding private-credit and BDC exposure face correlated NAV markdowns and possible NAIC/regulatory capital scrutiny, given ~35% of North American insurer portfolios are in private credit (IMF, 2025-26)

what_would_change_my_mind: Sub-fund-level leverage and liquidity data for major pension systems (not just aggregate funded ratios) would let me size the forced-flow effect precisely rather than infer it from funded-status headlines; also a direct NAIC or EIOPA breakdown of insurer private-credit losses realized (not just exposure) through the 2026 private-credit stress would sharpen the credibility score on loss-recognition.
